_about: Why each household is moving. 'line' is what they tell the clipboard; 'beats' are told in order while you work; 'ending' closes the results card. Party kinds: adult, elder, kid.

stories.title: Ilse's bungalow
stories.why: Walter died in the spring. The big house had too many stairs and too many of his coats.
stories.line: Walter's chair comes. The rest I've already given away twice.
beats: Forty-six years in the old place. I kept walking into his study to tell him things.
The clock was his father's. It loses four minutes a day and I set it back every morning. I'll keep doing that.
My daughter wanted me nearer. This is nearer. It has one floor and a garden I can manage, and that's enough.
stories.ending: Ilse sits in Walter's chair, looks at the window for a while, and says that will do nicely.

stories.title: The Okonkwos' move
stories.why: A third child is due in March and the flat had two bedrooms and one argument a night about them.
stories.line: Kitchen first. Then the cot. Then everything else, in no order at all.
beats: We found out in August. Grace said 'we need a house' before she said 'congratulations'. She was right.
The boys have shared a room since Tobi was born. Tobi says he is never sharing again. He will share with the baby.
The piano was Grace's mother's. Nobody plays it. It is coming anyway, because it is Grace's mother's.
stories.ending: Grace puts a hand on the piano, the boys fight over the back bedroom, and the Okonkwos are home.

stories.title: Maeve and Tom's first house
stories.why: Six years of renting, three landlords, one deposit never returned. The terrace is theirs, every creaking inch.
stories.line: Everything says FRAGILE because Tom panicked with the marker. Ignore most of it.
beats: We viewed it in the rain. Tom said the damp patch was 'character'. It was damp. It's fixed now. Mostly.
The last landlord kept our deposit for a mark on a wall that was there when we moved in. I have photos. I have so many photos.
Tom labelled the box with the kettle in it 'KETTLE, URGENT'. That one we're opening first.
stories.ending: Tom finds the box marked KETTLE, URGENT. Maeve finds the mugs. Nobody can take the house off them.

stories.title: The Reyes family's big move
stories.trade: family of three, from the coast
stories.why: Marco's job moved inland and the whole family came with it, one sulking eleven-year-old included.
stories.line: Four bedrooms to fill. The bunk beds are in bits. Sorry.
beats: Lucia hasn't spoken since the motorway. She left her best friend by the sea. We've promised a trip back every month.
The company paid for the move. We didn't pay for a crew this good, so thank you. I mean it.
There's a bedroom with a window seat. We haven't told Lucia it's hers yet. We're saving it.
stories.ending: Lucia finds the window seat on her own. She doesn't say anything, but she stays there, and that's a yes.

stories.title: Priya's flat
stories.why: Night shifts at the hospital and a forty-minute bus. The flat is four minutes on foot and that is the entire reason.
stories.line: One trip, I hope. The bed is the only heavy thing.
beats: I finished a thirteen-hour shift at seven this morning. Please don't tell me the box numbers twice.
My mother wanted me to buy a house with a garden. I want to sleep. Sleep won.
The bed goes against the wall with no window. I measured the light at six a.m. I'm not joking.
stories.ending: Priya closes the curtains, tests the bed, and is asleep before you've shut the van.

stories.title: The Lindgrens' townhouse
stories.why: Aunt Britt left them the townhouse in her will, with a note that said 'fix the roof and don't sell it'.
stories.line: The loft is for the train set. Do not tell my wife it is for the train set.
beats: Britt lived here fifty years. She left the house to us and her cat to the neighbour. The cat got the better deal, she said.
The roof is fixed. Cost more than the move. Britt would have said we were robbed and she'd have been right.
Elsa's grandad built the train set. It has never been fully set up. The loft is the right size. That's not a coincidence.
stories.ending: Elsa's grandad's train runs a full loop in the loft for the first time in thirty years. Britt would have approved of the roof.

stories.title: Mr Bello's cottage
stories.why: He fell off a ladder in his own orchard and his daughter said that was that. The cottage is two streets from her.
stories.line: The shed matters more than the house. Mower first.
beats: Forty years I had that orchard. One fall and suddenly I'm 'a worry'. I'm not a worry, I'm a man with a bruise.
She picked this place. Nice shed, I'll give her that. Garden's a handkerchief. I'll make it work.
Don't put the mower near the paint. The mower has never been near the paint. I have standards, even now.
stories.ending: Mr Bello inspects the shed, moves the mower two inches, and says 'fine' in a way that means thank you.

stories.title: Jun and Sol's loft
stories.why: The studio got three big clients in a year and the kitchen table stopped being an office.
stories.line: Open plan, so put things where they look right, not where they go.
beats: We started in Sol's bedroom with one laptop. Last month we hired someone. She needs a desk that isn't the sofa.
The brick wall is why we took it. Everything else is why we nearly didn't.
The telescope was Jun's dad's. It's not for stars. It's for pretending we can see the river from here.
stories.ending: Sol moves one chair a quarter-turn, Jun says nothing, and the loft is officially a studio.

stories.title: The Achebe twins' maisonette
stories.why: Second year, first place without a warden, and two of everything because neither will share.
stories.line: Two of everything, and we will argue about which is whose.
beats: Mum cried at the door. Dad checked the locks. We've been here one hour and the kettle's already contested.
Kemi gets the big bedroom because Kemi 'got better grades'. By two marks. Two.
We're going to be very tidy. We've agreed. We've written it down. It's on the fridge, which is mine, by the way.
stories.ending: The twins argue about the big bedroom for twenty minutes, then order a pizza and split it exactly in half.

stories.title: The Vargas move in with Grandad
stories.why: Grandad can't run the villa on his own any more and won't leave it, so the whole family is moving in with him.
stories.line: Three floors and a shed. Bring a flask.
beats: Dad built this house. Dad's not leaving this house. So here we all are, in Dad's house. Mind the paintwork, he'll notice.
The kids think it's a castle. The kids haven't seen the heating bill.
The shed's his. The loft's ours. The kitchen is a negotiation we haven't had yet.
stories.ending: Grandad stands at the top of his stairs, counts everyone in, and says the house finally sounds right.

stories.title: Mrs Castellano's new start
stories.why: Forty years in the family home. After Enzo, the rooms were too quiet and the garden too big.
stories.line: Half a house of things. Gentle with the photographs.
beats: The children were raised in the old house. I kept it two years after Enzo. I was keeping it for him, not for me.
I gave the dining table to my son. Twelve chairs. I need two.
The photographs go in the lounge, all of them, even the ugly one from 1979. Especially that one.
stories.ending: Mrs Castellano puts the photograph from 1979 where she can see it from the kitchen, and the house stops being empty.

stories.title: Dev and the boys
stories.why: The divorce went through in June. The terrace is small, near the school, and his.
stories.line: Bunk beds, a telly, and an unreasonable amount of football kit.
beats: It's been a year. Not a good one. This is the first thing that's been just ours.
They're with me weekdays, their mum weekends. The bunks go in the back room. The telly goes where they can't see it from bed.
I've got a list from their mum. It's a good list. Don't tell her I said that.
stories.ending: The boys claim the bunks, Dev finds the kettle, and the house is loud in the right way for once.

stories.title: The Haddads come home
stories.trade: family of three, back from abroad
stories.why: Ten years overseas for Samir's work. Teta is eighty-four and wanted to come home, so they all came home.
stories.line: We have been abroad ten years. The containers arrive today. All of them.
beats: Teta said she would like to see the river again before she goes. So we sold the apartment and here we are. She's fine. She'll outlive us.
Half of this is from the old country, half from the new one. None of it matches. That's the point.
The brass coffee set stays in its box until Teta is in her chair. Then she unwraps it. That's the rule.
stories.ending: Teta unwraps the brass coffee set herself, sets it on the table, and the Haddads are home in both senses.

stories.title: Noor and Amal's cottage
stories.why: The cottage was Amal's mother's. She left it to them with a leaking roof and a note that said 'now fix it'.
stories.line: The bath is cast iron. We know. We are sorry.
beats: Amal's mum lived here alone for twenty years and refused help with the roof. We fixed the roof. We cried a bit.
The bath was hers. It weighs more than the van. We considered leaving it. We couldn't.
We're keeping her rose by the shed. Everything else in the garden is up for debate.
stories.ending: Amal runs the first bath in the cast iron tub and says her mum would have been furious about the colour of the tiles.

stories.title: Teddy's smaller flat
stories.why: The warehouse closed in May. The flat is half the rent, and half the size, and Teddy would rather not talk about it.
stories.line: Not much. A bed, a telly, the good chair. Don't make a thing of it.
beats: Twelve years at the depot. Got a card and a cake. The cake was good, I'll say that.
Sold the car. Sold the bike. Kept the chair. A man needs one good chair.
There's an interview Thursday. Don't say good luck. People keep saying good luck.
stories.ending: Teddy sits in the good chair, looks at the smaller flat, and says it'll do for now. Thursday is Thursday.

stories.title: The Fontaine sisters move in together
stories.why: Both widowed within two years. They decided one house, two kettles, and no more rattling around alone.
stories.line: Two of everything, because we are not sharing a kettle at our age.
beats: We shared a bedroom until I was sixteen. Now we're sharing a house. It's taken fifty-eight years to get back here.
Her Gerald, my Henri. Within two years of each other. Terrible. And then we thought: well, why not?
She's having the bedroom at the front because she 'likes to see who's coming'. She's always liked to see who's coming.
stories.ending: The Fontaine sisters put two kettles on, side by side, and argue happily about which one boils first.

stories.title: Marisol's loft
stories.why: The band split, the relationship split, and the loft has a brick wall that sounds right when you play against it.
stories.line: The piano is the only thing that matters. Everything else is luggage.
beats: We were together nine years and in a band for seven of them. The band ended first. Should have seen that coming.
The loft was the first place I played a chord in and didn't hear him in it.
The piano goes against the brick. Not the plaster. The brick. I'll know.
stories.ending: Marisol plays one chord against the brick wall, listens to it ring, and nods. That's the whole review.

stories.title: The Brennans' bungalow
stories.why: Finn's chair doesn't do stairs. The bungalow has none, a wide hall, and a ramp Paul built himself.
stories.line: Wide doorways, no steps. Finn will tell you where his things go. Listen to him.
beats: We've been on the housing list two years. A bungalow came up. We cried in the car park.
Paul built the ramp over three weekends. It's slightly too steep. Finn has timed it. Finn times everything.
Finn's room is at the back because that's where the birds are. He asked for the birds first.
stories.ending: Finn takes the ramp at speed, declares it 'acceptable', and asks when the birds get here.

stories.title: Hal comes back to town
stories.why: He sold the hardware shop after forty years and came back to the town he grew up in, which has changed and he's not happy about it.
stories.line: There's a lot of tools. Don't touch the tools. I'll do the tools.
beats: Left this town at eighteen. Said I'd never come back. The shop's sold, the knees are gone, here I am.
The bakery's a phone shop now. The pub's flats. The river's still the river, I'll give it that.
My brother's two streets over. Haven't spoken in nine years. He doesn't know I'm here yet. That's a Thursday problem.
stories.ending: Hal sorts the toolbox by size before he unpacks a single plate. Then he walks two streets over, and comes back lighter.

stories.title: Three generations, one maisonette
stories.why: Baba's flat had no lift and her hips had opinions. Now she lives with them, downstairs, with the garden.
stories.line: Baba downstairs, us upstairs, Mio wherever Mio decides. Shoes off.
beats: Baba said she'd move in 'for a few weeks' after the operation. That was in February. We've stopped pretending.
Mio has been promised the room with the sloping ceiling. Mio is four and thinks it's a tent.
The kitchen's Baba's. We all know it's Baba's. The sign on the fridge is a formality.
stories.ending: Baba puts the sign on the fridge, Mio moves into her tent, and the maisonette settles into its new order.
